articles.text: On the morning of Friday, November 13, more than 300 people gathered in Piedmont Park to participate in the annual Ruby Bridges Walk to School event, hosted by the Affinity Mentors. The event honors Bridges’ historic November 14, 1960 walk into William Frantz Elementary School in New Orleans, a moment that helped challenge segregation nationwide. Bridges became the first African American student to desegregate an all-white school in the American South. Jean Takazawa, Piedmont Director of Diversity, Equity, Inclusion and Belonging, said she has been part of running this event for the past four years, originally partnering with a parent organization. Over the past four years, her Affinity Mentor class from Piedmont High School (PHS) has taken on the responsibility, having high school students speak and bring together the community each year. “We want to bring awareness to who Ruby Bridges was and the monumental historic event of what happened when she was a six year old girl walking into a white elementary school,” Takazawa said. “It’s important for our young people to learn history and honor those who have taken steps to become activists like that.” Affinity Mentor and junior Allyson Huynh said the Walk to School event provides a great opportunity for everyone to come together and celebrate the brave and historic action of a young girl. “I love getting to watch and support my fellow Affinity Mentorship classmates speak in front of the crowd,” Huynh said. articles.text: Piedmont Center for the Arts (PCA) opened at 801 Magnolia in 2011 with musicians Stuart Gronningen and Tom Reicher’s Horn Fanfare from the top of the grand stairway into the building. For 15 years, we have maintained a home for the arts in Piedmont benefiting our citizens, our artists, and our children. Led by community volunteers and Arts enthusiasts, the people of Piedmont now have a cultural space offering affordable access to art, music, lectures, drama, recitals, and rehearsals! Gray Cathrall donated an antique Steinway grand piano, rebuilt by the masters at Callahan Piano. It’s our Crown Jewel. We have attracted musicians from far and wide, and are known nationally and internationally by musicians and artists as a unique and welcoming venue. Support for the Arts competes with many other worthwhile endeavors. To meet this challenge for PCA, we are reaching out to all of you who support the Arts and believe Piedmont is culturally enriched through PCA activities and events. Help us so we can continue to attract the high quality performers and artists we’ve become known for. Please consider making a year-end donation to PCA! If you go to the following link on our website (https://www.piedmontcenterforthearts.org/get-involved) and click the “DONATE NOW” button, it’s easy to use and very secure. We are a 501(C)(3) Public Benefit non-profit corporation, so your gift is tax deductible. Please check out our website for upcoming events, follow our calendar in the Piedmont Post, and join our mailing list to get hot news! We hope to see you soon at Piedmont Center for the Arts. –Sue Malick President, Board of Directors Piedmont Center for the Arts, Inc.

articles.text: Piedmont, Albany, and Emeryville are the only three cities in Alameda County where voters do not directly elect their mayor. Instead, residents elect City Council members, who choose the mayor and vice mayor from among themselves. Piedmont’s mayor serves a two-year term, while those in Albany and Emeryville serve one-year terms. For at least 40 years, Piedmont has followed a tradition of choosing its mayor and vice mayor by seniority. The council will select its next leaders on December 7. Under the customary succession, current Vice Mayor Conna McCarthy is next in line to become mayor, while Council member Tom Ramsey, recently reelected to a second term, could become vice mayor. Piedmont’s mayor does not oversee the day-to-day administration of the city, but the position carries influence. In addition to presiding over City Council meetings and representing Piedmont at official functions, the mayor can help shape city priorities and champion major initiatives. At the first City Council meeting in December following each general election, council members elect the mayor and vice mayor. By tradition, the vice mayor becomes mayor, and the vice mayor’s position goes to the next most senior council member. If two members have served equally long, the number of votes received in their first council elections has been used to break the tie. But tradition is not binding. The council can choose someone else. Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen believes the system makes sense. In a small city like Piedmont, where Council members serve as volunteers, rotating the mayoral responsibilities every two years give members an opportunity to lead. The system has not always worked smoothly. In December 2020, Council members Jen Cavenaugh and Tim Rood, both serving their second terms, were considered for vice mayor. The question came down to how seniority should be determined and whether vote totals should break the tie. With Rood absent from the meeting, the council split 2-2 over appointing Cavenaugh as vice mayor. Council member Betsy Smegal Andersen proposed a compromise: Cavenaugh and Rood would each serve one year of the two-year vice mayoral term. The council approved the arrangement 3-1. The episode showed that the council can depart from its usual succession practice. On December 7, newly elected Council members Nancy Beninati and Bill Reichle will be sworn in alongside Ramsey, who won a second term earlier this month. The council will then vote on Piedmont’s next mayor and vice mayor.
articles.title: Piedmont is one of three Alameda County cities that don’t elect their mayor

articles.text: As winter temperatures and rains befall the Bay Area, Wildwood third grade Girl Scouts of Troop 32125 are teaming up with Girl Scouts of Northern California and One Warm Coat to share warmth. Troop 32125 is asking area residents to look through their closets for a clean coat or jacket in good condition that’s ready for a new home. Donations make an immediate impact in the local community by providing those in need with a tangible gift, protection from the elements. Donations of coats and jackets are being accepted through November 30. “It’s part of our Girl Scout oath to help others. We are happy to help less fortunate people who don’t have warm coats for the winter,” said Girl Scout Siena Paley. The troop is hoping to collect at least 50 coats, which will be donated to Community Action Alliance, an Oakland nonprofit that provides housing and economic support in partnership with One Warm Coat. Last year, more than 4,000 individuals, organizations and companies across the country worked with One Warm Coat to collect nearly 500,000 coats, which were distributed to children and adults in need across the United States. “This project brings me joy. I really like helping less fortunate people find coats. Make sure to donate a coat!” said Girl Scout Hayden Driskill. Coats can be dropped off outside the front doors of Wildwood Elementary or on the porches of 1042 Annerley Road or 154 Wildwood Gardens. Coats are needed in all sizes, but especially men’s coats and jackets. About One Warm Coat Founded in 1992 by one woman with one coat to give, One Warm Coat is a national nonprofit organization that originated with one simple act of kindness. With a deep-seated belief in the power of collective action, One Warm Coat engages and supports thousands of volunteers each year to collect coats, sharing warmth with half a million people in need in communities nationwide. Over the past 33 years, One Warm Coat has distributed nearly 9 million coats through a network of 1,500 local nonprofit partners, keeping more than 22 million pounds of textiles out of landfills. Visit onewarmcoat.org today to learn how individuals and organizations can engage with One Warm Coat’s mission to share warmth, not waste. Girl Scout Troop 32125 crafted this donation box to accept winter coats for those in need. Donations can be made in front of Wildwood School or on the porches of 1042 Annerley Road and 154 Wildwood Gardens.

articles.text: The Piedmont City Council voted unanimously on Monday, November 16, to begin negotiating an exclusive negotiation agreement (ENA) with Eden Housing and City Ventures to develop new housing in Moraga Canyon. An ENA would establish a formal process for the city and development team to evaluate site conditions, refine development plans, and negotiate the terms of a potential development agreement. This vote is a big step toward the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan as part of Piedmont’s state-mandated housing obligations. In May, the city issued a Request for Qualifications (RFQ) seeking an experienced development partner. The city only received one response to the RFQ from Eden Housing and City Ventures. Council member Tom Ramsey asked Planning Director Leslie Mendez how the process changed with only one applicant. “We still had the template of what we were looking for in a development team through the qualifications listed in the RFQ. The selection committee pivoted from an evaluation to a deep dive. This gave us the confidence to move forward with this recommendation. We do not believe going out further would heighten the quality we received,” said Mendez. The selection committee assessed Eden Housing and City Ventures’ capabilities with two rounds of interviews, a review of financial capacity and experience, and a review of their established track record. After three months of review, the committee determined the applicants are a highly capable development team with the experience, financial capacity, and track record needed to deliver a high-quality project that reflects the community’s vision. Many residents spoke at the meeting, voicing their support for the project. Resident Sarah Karlinski shared her thoughts on the project during the public comment. “I think that Eden Housing, the development team, is incredibly strong. I am very excited about the idea of living in an inclusive community where we can live together. People from different backgrounds. Different walks of life, different economic conditions. I think that’s going to be good for this city.” Resident Ralph Catalano urged the council to postpone the vote until they held a public hearing with the community about the preferred location of the building. Other residents expressed their concerns regarding traffic safety and the potential use of cemetery land. The development team’s preliminary proposal includes 132 homes on the south side of Moraga Avenue, with 81 affordable apartments and 51 market-rate townhomes. Potential development of future parcels on Abbott Way and Maxwelton Road is proposed following further investigation of the topography. The Eden/City Ventures proposal identifies Eden Housing as the lead developer and responsible for affordable housing, while City Ventures would be responsible for market-rate housing. City Ventures has developed townhome projects in Novato, Moraga, Morgan Hill, Oakland, San Mateo, and Sunnyvale, as well as mixed-use and single-family home projects throughout the region. Eden Housing launched in 1968 and has over 12,000 units across California. Its most recent projects include a $66 million project in Castro Valley, a $70 million project in Mountain View, and two projects in Fremont amounting to $43 million and $38 million. The vote does not commit the city to any specific project; it authorizes the city to negotiate terms with the development team. Specific development plans, land use approvals, and any potential transfer of city-owned land would be subject to future Council review and approval, with additional opportunities for public engagement.
articles.title: Piedmont to start negotiations with developers for Moraga Canyon Specific Plan

articles.text: As we wrap up our first PHS water polo season at Piedmont’s beautiful new community pool, after seven years without a home pool, we have a lot to be thankful for. Back in 2020, Piedmont voters approved Measure UU and its promise of “greater community access,” including a larger pool “for lap swimming and competitive sports.” Six years later, here we are, and it’s amazing! A big thank-you to Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen, who championed that vision from her early days on the Recreation Commission all the way to the ribbon-cutting, and to the many volunteers and city leaders who made it real. This Thanksgiving, we’re especially grateful for: • Walking down our neighborhood sidewalks to practice, right in the heart of Piedmont. • Five home games, with family, friends, teachers and neighbors cheering us on and discovering this crazy game of water polo. • Celebrating Senior Night at HOME, complete with banners and a scoreboard. • Our coaches, whose dedication goes far beyond the pool deck. • Chelle, Paula, Hadley and the entire PRD staff, for their patience, flexibility and hard work making practices and home games happen while keeping community programs running. And we’re thankful for what’s ahead. In our very first season home, our varsity team finished third in the WACC and earned a move up to Division 1. Three girls played varsity alongside the boys, and ten more trained with the team all season. With a big group of returning athletes, we’re just getting started. If you build it, they will come. Just ask the Golden State Valkyries, who showed the whole Bay Area what happens when a community gives a team a home. Our

articles.text: Good morning and welcome to KidNuz. Today is Wednesday, November 18, 2026, and we begin with Polar Night falling on America’s northernmost city. Utqiagvik, Alaska sits 320 miles above the Arctic Circle. At 1:42 local time this afternoon, because of the tilt of the Earth, the sun will dip below the horizon — and won’t rise above it for 65 long, dark days. The temperature drops right along with the sun, with the average daytime high hovering around minus eight degrees. The tables turn on January 23, 2027, when the sun makes its first re-appearance above the horizon. It won’t stay up long at first, only about an hour, but its presence will mark the start of the transition to the 24/7 daylight season known as Midnight Sun, which officially begins in May. Maybe banning cell phones in class DOES work. Previous studies have shown mixed results, but according to the New York Times, the first, large national study actually shows an improvement in test scores. The just-released Harvard research looked at 3.3 million third through tenth graders between 2021 and 2026 and found that schools with the strictest bans — where students had to lock their phones in pouches all day — saw math and reading scores improve as if students had an additional week or two of school a year. Schools with less strict bans also improved, just not as much. If you’re hitting the road with family for the holiday, you won’t be alone, but it’s also not going to be quite as crowded as years past. According to AAA, 81.5 million Americans will travel more than 50 miles from home between next Tuesday and the Monday after Thanksgiving. That’s a smidge lower than last year — a tenth of a percent to be exact. If AAA’s travel forecast holds, the small drop would end three years of record-setting Thanksgiving travel. Back in 2020, Piedmont voters approved Measure UU and its promise of “greater community access,” including a larger pool “for lap swimming and competitive sports.” Six years later, here we are, and it’s amazing! A big thank-you to Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen, who championed that vision from her early days on the Recreation Commission all the way to the ribbon-cutting, and to the many volunteers and city leaders who made it real. This Thanksgiving, we’re especially grateful for: • Walking down our neighborhood sidewalks to practice, right in the heart of Piedmont. A Water Polo Thanksgiving • Five home games, with family, friends, teachers and neighbors cheering us on and discovering this crazy game of water polo. • Celebrating Senior Night at HOME, complete with banners and a scoreboard. • Our coaches, whose dedication goes far beyond the pool deck. • Chelle, Paula, Hadley and the entire PRD staff, for their patience, flexibility and hard work making practices and home games happen while keeping community programs running. And we’re thankful for what’s ahead. In our very first season home, our varsity team finished third in the WACC and earned a move up to Division 1. Three girls played varsity alongside the boys, and ten more trained with the team all season. With a big group of returning athletes, we’re just getting started. If you build it, they will come. Just ask the Golden State Valkyries, who showed the whole Bay Area what happens when a community gives a team a home. Our goal is a Piedmont program that competes in Division 1 year after year, and this pool makes that possible. In the spirit of Measure UU’s promise of greater community access, our next step is working with the City and PRD on youth clinics, so younger kids, especially girls, can discover the sport long before high school. Water polo builds strength, confidence and grit, and teaches kids to work hard for each other. We can’t wait to build on this momentum. To the City of Piedmont and everyone who made this pool possible: thank you. There’s no place like home, especially when home has a water polo pool. Maybe banning cell phones in class DOES work. Previous studies have shown mixed results, but according to the New York Times, the first, large national study actually shows an improvement in test scores. The just-released Harvard research looked at 3.3 million third through tenth graders between 2021 and 2026 and found that schools with the strictest bans — where students had to lock their phones in pouches all day — saw math and reading scores improve as if students had an additional week or two of school a year. Schools with less strict bans also improved, just not as much. articles.text: After a year of not performing at PHS, Troubadours will once again be singing this winter, spreading holiday cheer among students. After functioning independently from PHS but still performing for Holiday-O-Grams and Heart-O-Grams since 2019, Troubadours faced issues last year with administration regarding equity as a student-run organization, said Troubadour and junior Audrey Levin. “From my understanding, the Troubadours had been able to be almost completely independent since the old choir director left, but were still allowed to sing at school for Heart-O-Grams, Holiday-O-Grams, and other events,” Levin said. “Then under the current school administration, administrators realized there were legal issues with equity in a completely student-run group and had certain conditions for how Troubs would have to change to keep singing at the school.” Although Troubadours did not participate in school-affiliated events last year, they continued to function as an independent, student-run group. After continuing to work with administration, they have reached a compromise and will return to PHS as a semischool affiliated group. “This year’s senior directors were able to find a different compromise where Troubs can remain independent and student run, but have a music teacher present at auditions and some rehearsals to make sure they’re fair,” Levin said. “Now we’ll probably be able to sing at school events like before!” This year, Troubadours held auditions with a school faculty member present to ensure fairness, and they now have rehearsals on campus once a week, Levin said. “We are still able to do independent activities such as having student leaders, Sunday rehearsals, fall retreat, and gigs, but this compromise allows us to have a connection with the school so we can begin singing at school again,” Levin said. “Troubadours also have weekly on-campus practices in the music room every Friday,” said junior Mara Pisani. “We still can do paid off-campus gigs in smaller groups, like how jazz band has smaller groups that perform off campus,” Pisani said. Levin said she enjoys the community that comes from Troubadours. “Especially after we have our fall retreat, in which we spend a weekend learning music and being in nature,” Levin said. All of the Troubadours are very excited to be singing on campus again for Heart-O-Grams and Holiday-O-Grams, Pisani said. She emphasized the bonds that she has with her fellow Troubadours are very special. “It’s like a family,” Pisani said. Julia Stokes is a junior at Piedmont High School and a student writer intern for the Piedmont Post. Piedmont’s Troubadours prepare for a musical 2026 holiday season. articles.text: Performances of Peter Pan and Wendy filled the Alan Harvey Theater for each of the four performances Thursday-Saturday, November 12-14. Piedmont High School’s Advanced Acting class performed Lauren Gunderson’s reimagined look at J.M. Barrie’s classic 1911 Peter Pan with swordfighting bravado, amazing aerial stunts and on-the-nose societal commentary that brought the joy of Neverland to all in witness. Hundreds of audience members escaped the rain and stormed the theater, offering a true primetime playhouse experience for audience members and Director Kim Taylor’s cast. Gunderson’s version, with some modernized themes, premiered at Shakespeare Theater in Washington D.C. in 2019. The opening scene of the play transported audience members to Wendy’s bedroom and balcony, as Peter Pan, played by junior Miles Simon, tried to find his shadow. Simon put his stamp on the major role of Pan, in just his first year of acting and first PHS production. Junior Lucy Shoop, in her first advanced acting play at Piedmont High School (PHS), navigated the multitude of roles for Wendy with extraordinary grace. She cohesively stitched together Wendy in all her complexity as de facto mother, sister, daughter and scientist-to-be. When Wendy found out that her parents planned to send her to finishing school, Wendy lamented the decision in soliloquy. Her query of “why would parents want to ‘finish’ their children anyway,” produced a wave of chuckles from the parents in the stands. Aliana Tejeda, in her first ever production, did a wonderful job giving ferocity and life to the updated and more formidable character, Tiger Lily. In a thoughtful plot change from the original, instead of Peter Pan rescuing Tiger Lily from drowning, Tiger Lily actively saves an unconscious Peter Pan from his doom. A standout performance also came from Zayd Mahmood as Captain Hook. Mahmood’s experience in musical roles, including Kenickie in Grease and Prince Eric in The Little Mermaid, resulted in his commanding stage presence. articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ tennis team fell in a narrow 4-3 battle with No. 8 Alameda in the Division 1 North Coast Section Team Tournament at the Hornets’ home court on Tuesday, November 10. It was a match that pitted two Western Alameda County Conference schools against each other. The Highlanders and Hornets split their regular season matches, a 4-3 loss to Alameda on October 14 and a 5-2 victory on October 28. “It was a tough loss as we had just beaten Alameda 5-2 two weeks ago,” coach Jim Landes said. Piedmont won three of four singles matches, but lost all three at doubles to concede the day. At singles, Ella Ruthven won 6-2, 6-3 at the No. 1 spot, while Faith Chin won by the same score at No. 2. Maddy Huynh, a freshman, won her No. 3 match in straight sets by scores of 6-2, 6-1. “Ella Ruthven, Faith Chin and Maddy Huynh all won convincingly in straight sets. This was particularly good for Faith, who needed a third set tiebreak to win against the same opponent two weeks earlier,” Landes said. But a big switch from the previous two encounters with Alameda was their No. 4 singles starter, Natalia Gilbert, beating Leela Sivakumar 6-1, 6-4. Sivakumar had defeated Glbert in both of their previous matches by scores of 6-4, 5-7, 10-5 on October 28 and 6-3, 6-2 on October 14. “Leela Sivakumar lost this time in straight sets against Natalie Gilbert. who she had defeated in both previous encounters. Natalie played extremely well this day making very few unforced errors,” Landes said. Alameda ultimately flipped the day with its three doubles wins, winning all three matches in straight sets. The Hornets also won all three doubles matches in their October 14 victory against Piedmont. “Alameda’s strength is in their doubles and on this day it showed,” Landes said. PHS’ No. 1 team of Emma Chan and Chiara Silvio fell in a heated 6-4, 7-6 (7-5) bout. Ella Thomasson and Mai Pham lost 6-4, 6-1 at No. 2, while Amelia Oldrin and Amalia Angulo lost 6-1, 6-4. Oldrin and Angulo previously beat Alameda in three sets on October 28. “Emma and Chiara battled and took their opponents to a tiebreak in the second set but went down 7-5. Ella Thomasson and Mai Pham, and Amelia Oldrin and Amalia Angulo did not fare as well. In the previous encounter with Alameda, both of our teams had three-set battles with Amelia and Amalia winning. Alameda’s girls played some excellent tennis and proved too much on this day,” Landes said. But Piedmont’s season isn’t over just yet. Ruthven competed in the Division 2 NCS Individual Tournament’s singles ladder, while Chan and Chin played in the doubles bracket. Ruthven, Chan, and Chin each won their first-round match on Monday, November 16, while Tuesday’s matches were not completed by Post time. NCS Individual Tournament details. articles.text: Eight honorees to be inducted at ceremony on April 24, 2027 The Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame today announced its Class of 2027, an eight-member group of honorees whose achievements span the football field, the track, the pool, the tennis court, and beyond. The inductees will be formally recognized at the PSHOF’s induction ceremony on April 24, 2027, at the Alan Harvey Theater. This year’s class includes standout athletes, a dedicated coach, a multi-category honoree and remarkable pioneers of women’s sports. Together, their combined legacies reflect decades of excellence, leadership, and service to Piedmont High School athletics. The Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame Class of 2027 includes: • Michael Hernandez (Class of 2012) — Lacrosse. Piedmont’s all-time scoring leader at the time he graduated, a Division I All-American at Michigan, and a professional and international player and coach. • Steve Humphries (Class of 1985) — A triple-category inductee honored for more than 35 years as a player, coach, and community volunteer. • Melissa “Missy” Moore Berger (Class of 1983) — Track & Field. A state-level 800-meter runner whose Piedmont record has stood for nearly five decades. • Doyle O’Regan — Teacher, Cross Country & Track Coach. A 22-year coaching leader who built one of the Bay Area’s most consistently competitive track programs and founder of the Annual Piedmont Turkey Trot. • Nick Pacult (Class of 2017) — Football, Swimming, Basketball. Piedmont’s all-time leading tackler and a three-sport standout and league champion. • Rebecca “Becky” Richter (Class of 1980) — Basketball, Softball, Volleyball. A 12-letter athlete and early pioneer of girls’ and women’s sports at Piedmont. • “Betsy” Swan Diaz (Class of 1983) — Soccer, Softball, Volleyball. An 11-letter, three-sport captain who went on to a Division I soccer career, an engineering career at Apple, and elite marathon running. • Kaelli Thiel (Class of 2016) — Tennis. A four-time league champion and Ivy League tennis standout recognized equally for scholarship and service. The Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame (PSHOF) was established in 2003 by a group of citizens with a keen interest in the rich athletic history of Piedmont High School. The Hall of Fame was founded upon the principle that Piedmont High School athletes, coaches, administrators, boosters and community members who have made outstanding contributions to PHS athletics should be honored and enshrined. The public is invited to join in celebrating the Class of 2027 at the induction ceremony on Saturday, April 24, 2027. Additional details on tickets and event logistics will be announced separately. Learn more about the 2027 class and ceremony updates at www.psfof.org.

articles.text: Staff Photos Oakland Roots received unanimous approval to build a new stadium on Bay Farm Island in Alameda, but seek $15 million from new investors. It’s a precarious time for the last remaining professional sports team in the East Bay. Oakland Roots SC competes in the second division of American soccer in the USL Championship and recently secured approval to host games at their training facility on Bay Farm Island in Alameda, which used to house the former Oakland Raiders. Roots plan to build an 8,000 capacity stadium at the site with the aim of playing there for a maximum of five years as they secure their permanent stadium at Howard Terminal. However, the club has an important caveat toward finalizing its future – they need $15 million in new investments or they could be in peril. In recent weeks, The Athletic’s Marcus Thompson wrote that Oakland Roots are facing the unimaginable after speaking with figureheads at the organization. “The Roots say they need $15 million to finally capture more of the money their popularity generates. Without it, the club must start grappling with the reality that the future that once felt so certain coul-d evaporate before it reaches it,” Thompson wrote. “… Thus, a homegrown franchise born to galvanize a city at its sports nadir is struggling to find deep pockets to fund its mission… Their fate is now tied to the hope that someone wealthy cares about this as much as the community they’ve built. Maybe that’s the most damning indictment of what professional sports have become. The Oakland Roots have what we love most about sports. But the business of sports keeps reminding us — love might no longer live here.” The organization finds itself in a hole due to its nomadic existence, playing at properties they never owned since its inception in 2019. Roots played its inaugural 2019 season at Laney College in 2019, played there for one match in 2020 before the pandemic, and faced complications with their field in 2021. The Oakland club played at Las Positas in Livermore in 2021, returned to Laney in 2022, but another complication with Laney’s field renovation forced them to Cal State East Bay in 2023 and 2024. Then in 2025, Roots moved to the Oakland Coliseum, which pushed them deeper into a financial hole despite selling over 26,000 tickets for its 2025 season opener – a historic number for the USL Championship. Now entering 2027, the club revealed they’ve had $75 million in expenses due to their field situation, and require new big-money investors to make sure their shortterm stay in Bay Farm Island and long-term vision at Howard Terminal become a reality. On November 9, Alameda’s Planning Board has unanimously voted to approve Oakland Roots’ proposal for a temporary stadium at its training facility for up to a five-year term. The proposal’s draft resolution calls for Roots and its women’s team, the Soul, to host up to 27 professional soccer matches, along with “several small sporting events.” These smaller events could include youth and high school sporting events, like North Coast Section or CIF State Championship games. With the USL Championship 2027 season approaching in March, the clock is ticking on getting the stadium ready for the start. The club provided an update on its construction timeline, including site preparation through the end of November into January 2027, while they will transition into installing lighting and grand stands from January to March. Roots ruled out playing at seven other locations, including Kezar Stadium in San Francisco, the College of Alameda, Merritt College, Edwards Field in Berkeley, Cal State East Bay in Hayward, Laney College, and continuing at the Coliseum. Oakland Roots plan to build an 8,000 seat capacity stadium at its training facility, which is the same former practice site of the Oakland Raiders.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of San Francisco Museum of Modern Art RM x SFMOMA: Between You and Me is on view now. The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) presents an exhibition featuring nearly 180 works from the personal art collection of RM, the leader of South Korean pop group BTS, alongside works from the museum’s collection. RM x SFMOMA: Between You and Me is on view now through February 7, 2027. The exhibition is the first museum presentation of RM’s collection and its only U.S. showing. Curated by RM, whose full name is Kim Namjoon, with SFMOMA co-curators América Castillo and Hyoeun Kim, the exhibition brings together modern and contemporary works by Korean and international artists. Some works from RM’s collection have never been publicly exhibited in the United States. The exhibition pairs works from the two collections to explore themes including nature, memory and human existence, highlighting how artists from different backgrounds and periods have approached similar subjects. RM said he hopes the exhibition will encourage visitors to consider different perspectives and serve as a connection between cultures. “I don’t want to prescribe how these works should be seen; whether out of curiosity or study, all perspectives are welcome,” RM said in a press release. “My only hope is that this exhibition can be a small but sturdy bridge for many.” Works from RM’s collection include pieces by Korean artists Chang Ucchin, Kim Yun Shin, Kwon Okyon, Park Rehyun, To Sangbong and Yun Hyong-keun, as well as contemporary artists from around the world. The SFMOMA collection is represented by works from artists including Donald Judd, Kim Whanki, Yves Klein, Agnes Martin, Henri Matisse, Georgia O’Keeffe, Nam June Paik and Mark Rothko. The exhibition also will include an audio guide in English and Korean recorded by RM, along with bilingual wall texts and labels written by him. A playlist curated by RM will accompany the artworks in the galleries. More information about the exhibition and tickets is available at sfmoma.org/exhibition/rm-xsfmoma.

articles.text: Filoli’s annual holiday celebration returns this week, bringing more than 350,000 lights, a new family farm and holiday displays to the historic Woodside estate. “Holidays at Filoli” runs now through January 10 and includes daytime and evening activities across the 654-acre property. The estate has already sold more than 26,000 tickets for this year’s event, according to Filoli. Every year in November, Filoli’s decorating team installs and decorates 22 trees, 3,600 light strands that stretch more than 18 miles, over 7,000 luminescent ornaments, and 1,000 feet of festive garlands. The Reception Room’s 18-foot ceilings create an appropriate abode for “The Grand Tree,” the tallest of those on display. The two-story historic mansion contains 56 rooms, including a large ballroom and reception room designed to host concerts and debut balls. Each room in the mansion is adorned with holiday decorations that complement the room’s original hues and aesthetics. The design team carefully recreates the original holiday placement that is indicative of Agnes and William Bourn, the house’s first residents. New this year, the Filoli Family Farm will feature miniature cows, goats, sheep, piglets and a mother donkey with her baby. The farm will be located among the estate’s redwoods and will be open to daytime visitors. The attraction draws on Filoli’s history as a working country estate. The redwood railway also will return as part of Thistlewyck Village, a holiday-themed attraction with miniature trains, an Elf Academy and opportunities for children to write letters to the North Pole and take an oath with one of the village’s elves. Visitors can purchase a Thistlewyck Passport add-on that includes an elf hat, toy train and hot chocolate. Inside the Historic House, this year’s theme, Celtic Connections, will feature holiday decorations inspired by the Bourn family’s Irish heritage. William Bowers Bourn II, who built Filoli, purchased Muckross House in Killarney, Ireland, as a wedding gift for his daughter Maud and her husband in 1911. The decorations will include tartans, evergreen garlands, decorated trees and wreaths. Evening visitors can see more than 350,000 lights throughout the gardens, including a 210-foot light tunnel, illuminated orbs and glowing flower displays. The lights will be arranged across 28 miles of strands. The event will offer separate daytime and evening admission. Daytime visits, which include access to the Historic House, gardens, railway and family farm, will be available from 10 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., with last admission at 1:30 p.m. Evening light displays will run from 4 to 10 p.m., with last admission at 8 p.m. Filoli also will host Holiday Teas from December 1-18 at select times. The family-style afternoon teas will include tiered treats and sparkling wine in the Historic Garden House. Visit https://filoli.org/ to learn more and to purchase daytime or evening admission. Filoli Historic House and Garden is dressing up for the holidays.

articles.text: Visitors to the Crab Cove Visitor Center in Alameda can watch staff feed the center’s aquariums every Saturday and Sunday. The East Bay Regional Park District, which operates Crab Cove and the adjacent Robert W. Crown Memorial State Beach, will host its next feeding demonstration Saturday, November 21, at 3 p.m. Visitors can watch crabs, fish and other aquatic animals as they eat. Park district staff will explain what the animals eat and discuss the species and their habitats. Crab Cove houses San Francisco Bay wildlife in an 800-gallon aquarium system. The visitor center also features interactive exhibits for different age groups, including stations where visitors can view microscopic organisms, assemble a model crab and explore the mudflats from the perspective of a lugworm. The exhibits offer visitors an opportunity to learn about the underwater environment of San Francisco Bay. Photo courtesy of East Bay Regional Park District The feeding demonstrations are free and do not require registration. Crab Cove Visitor Center is open Wednesday through Sunday from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. November through February and from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. March through October. The center is closed on Thanksgiving, Christmas Eve, Christmas Day and New Year’s Day. For more information, call 510-544-3187 or visit https:// www.ebparks.org/.

articles.text: BeHere / 1942 is on view now through Dec. 27 A new exhibition at the Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) features historic photographs to examine the forced incarceration of Japanese Americans during World War II. BeHere / 1942: A New Lens on the Japanese American Incarceration, by Japanese artist Masaki Fujihata, is on view in the museum’s Great Hall now through December 27. The exhibition focuses on the period in 1942 before Japanese Americans in Oakland, San Francisco and Los Angeles were forcibly removed and sent to incarceration camps. Fujihata spent years researching photographs taken by Dorothea Lange and Russell Lee, who documented the removal and incarceration of Japanese Americans in the Bay Area and Los Angeles, respectively. The exhibition enlarges and animates selected images, encouraging visitors to examine the expressions of people photographed and the relationship Photo courtesy of Oakland Museum of California A museum patron views BeHere / 1942: A New Lens on the Japanese American Incarceration. between photographers and their subjects. The Oakland presentation includes installations based on Lange’s 1942 photographs of San Francisco and Oakland, including some taken across the street from the museum. A new three-screen video features local residents, some with personal connections to Japanese American incarceration and others affected by contemporary anti-immigrant policies. The exhibition also extends into Oak Street Plaza, where a life-size photograph of Japanese Americans preparing to board buses serves as the basis for an augmented reality experience. Visit https://museumca.org/ for more information.

articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Department’s new Piedmont Singin’ 4 Fun group had its first singing session last Tuesday, November 10, from 11 a.m. to noon at 801 Magnolia, the Piedmont Center for the Arts. The first meeting drew an excellent turnout of 29 singers. Activity organizer Dick Carter led the session off with a welcome and some information. He emphasized that the group’s primary objective is to have fun and to build community. He said it is important to understand that while the group’s singing will be good, it should not be expected that it will be concert quality. Participants don’t need to be good singers to be part of this group. They just have to enjoy singing together. For those in the group who are good singers, Dick asked that they please tolerate him. Besides having fun, another of the group’s objectives is to build community. Knowing each other’s names is an important part of this, and participants will have the option of wearing name badges provided by the Recreation Department to make this easier. The plan for the sessions is to start with participants introducing themselves and answering a quick personal question. The intent is to start the process of getting to know one another. For this first session, the question was, “Where did you go to high school?” By chance, two singers discovered they went to the same Southern California school years apart. After the introduction, there will be a short vocal warm-up, and then the session singing leader will get the group singing fun, popular songs. With all this shared, it was time for Marianne Jakus to lead the vocal warm-up. She had the group climb the octaves with “Do A Deer A Female Deer …” Appropriately limbered up, the singing was turned over to session leader Sarah Pearson. She had her Spotify account playlist queued up and ready for background music, and the singing began with Puff, the Magic Dragon. They were looking forward to their second Piedmont Singin’ 4 Fun session on November 17 at 11 a.m. Piedmont Singin’ 4 Fun will meet every Tuesday at 11 a.m. However, participants don’t need to come to every session. articles.text: Thanksgiving Day is meant for family, feasting, and being grateful. Nothing mars a happy occasion like mishaps involving your furry friend. Hosting family and cooking up a storm are stressful enough on their own, so let’s consider some ways to manage your dog on this cozy holiday. Following some simple food rules will help avoid digestive disasters during the holiday. Be sure to keep toxic ingredients, including chocolate, onions, limes, garlic, grapes, raisins, macadamia nuts, and artificial sweeteners like xylitol away from your pup. When treating your dog, skip the fatty foods. Turkey skin, butter, gravies, and rich sauces may cause severe stomach upset or even trigger pancreatitis (inflammation of the pancreas). Tempting as it may be, keep all bones out of reach. Cooked poultry bones can easily splinter, causing choking hazards, dangerous blockages, or cuts in the digestive tract. No one wants a pet ER visit on a holiday! Finally, be sure to instruct your visitors not to slip sneaky scraps to your dog under the table so you can be fully aware of everything your dog consumes. Securing the environment on a holiday is just as important as using safe judgment around treats. While rushing to get the feast on the table, you won’t be able to supervise your dog 100% of the time. Because of this, it is essential to make sure your trash is puppy-proof. Turkey carcasses, bones, string, and foil may be tempting for even the most well-behaved dog, so keep trash cans tightly covered or hidden. Also, be sure to watch the doors. With people coming and going, remind your guests to be careful when opening doors so your dog doesn’t slip outside without your knowledge. Just in case, make sure their ID tags and microchip information are up to date. Through all the chaos of Thanksgiving Day, don’t forget to give your dog the care they need. Take your pup on a long walk or play a vigorous game of fetch before guests arrive to help burn off extra energy. Then, set up a quiet, designated room or crate with familiar bedding, water, and toys where your dog can escape the noise and chaos of the day. Just like humans, dogs can become burnt out at family gatherings, too! Thanksgiving is a time for food, giving thanks, and family—including our four-legged friends! By keeping harmful foods out of reach, securing trash and doors, and providing your pup with exercise and a place to decompress, you can help make the holiday safe and enjoyable for everyone. Remember, the best Thanksgiving treat you can give your dog is a little extra care and attention. Wishing you and your furry friends a pawsome Thanksgiving! She helped to launch the service dog and facility dog training organization Alpha Dog Assist in Mill Valley in 2021 and currently offers private training in service dog work, obedience, and behavioral consultation. articles.text: Ask Scouts what they love about Scouts BSA, and you’ll get different answers—but friendship, personal growth, new challenges, and a sense of accomplishment run through them all. Here’s what three Piedmont Scouts have to say: Camille Hauser “My favorite memory from Scouting is going to Catalina Island with my troop. It was such a fun experience because I got to spend time with my friends while also trying new things and being outside in the water which is what I love most. That trip is one of the reasons I love Scouting so much. There are so many opportunities to do things that I wouldn’t normally get to do, from camping and backpacking to learning new skills and taking on leadership roles. I also like that Scouting gives me the chance to be around people of different ages and learn from them. Over the past two years, Scouts has helped me become more independent and confident while giving me some of my best memories. I don’t think I could get the same combination of adventure, responsibility, and community anywhere else.” Felix Kansal “One thing I really enjoy about Scouting is our long backpacking trips, particularly Troop 4’s annual 50-miler. I love the incredible views you get from being high in the mountains. Camille Hauser (middle) with Troop 15 Scoutmaster Jen Gregovich and Evie Luskin, 25-mile hike in Desolation Wilderness, at Lake of the Woods, July 2025 Sometimes it feels like you can see across an entire park without another soul in sight. Nature is beautiful, with alpine lakes and even snow in the summer. After such a long trek, you always feel proud of yourself and find it hard to believe you actually did it. Another rewarding part of Scouting is helping younger Scouts advance through the ranks. When you’re a young Scout, you hear, “He’s an Eagle Scout” or “She has 30 merit badges,” and those accomplishments seem almost impossible. But as you grow older, you realize those goals might not be so impossible, and then you’re the one inspiring the younger Scouts. I have also really enjoyed the Order of the Arrow. It’s expanded my Scouting journey as well as my commitment to community service, spending hours volunteering for others.” Travers Kemp “One of the neatest things about Scouting is how it’s been able to grow with me. When I first started, all I wanted to do was have fun with my friends messing around in tents and going on camping trips without my parents. articles.text: We plan a two-week vacation down to the dinner reservations. We don’t plan the next twenty years. I share that line every time I speak with seniors and their families, and the room always goes quiet. When I ask who has booked a restaurant for a trip months away, hands shoot up. When I ask who has a written plan for where they will live, who will manage things, and what will happen to everything in the house, very few hands go up. In more than 35 years as a realtor, I have walked alongside so many families through a parent’s move, a loss, or a long overdue downsizing. Right now we are working with four families in which the wife is living with dementia, and it has fallen to the husbands and the children to figure out what comes next. More often than not, that conversation turns into an argument. The difference between a stressful transition and a peaceful one almost always comes down to one thing: when they started. That is why I created Your Next Best Chapter, a one-day course for seniors and the families who love them, taking place January 30 at Piedmont Adult School. Nothing about planning ahead requires a decision today. It simply requires getting started. The way I help people get started is the same way I trained for my first marathon, a few months shy of my 60th birthday. I was not a runner at allbut I had the Mindset In Motion Method™. Earlier this year I published Mindset In Motion™: Activate Purpose, Power, and Peak Performance. Since then, I have been sharing the core concept of the book, the Mindset In Motion Method™, a five-step framework to help you through any transition: overcoming a loss, moving into a new chapter, conquering a personal or professional goal, or simply pushing yourself to Activate. So, take out a notepad and start outlining a plan for your future, while you are still in control of it. Five Steps, Any Goal • Goal. Get clear on exactly what you want. • Believe. Tell yourself it is possible, and that it is never too early to begin. • Internalize. Feel how it will feel once you are there. • Share. Bring in the people who will help you. • Activate. Take one concrete step this week. Here is how it works for two of the biggest pieces of any next chapter. Here’s one example: Purging • Goal. Picture a home filled only with the things you use and love every day. Not • • • • empty, just lighter. Believe. You do not need a moving date to begin. In fact, having no deadline is a gift. The people who feel the least stress on moving day are the ones who started years before, a little at a time. Internalize. Imagine opening a closet and seeing only what matters. Imagine the peace of knowing your children will never have to sort through a lifetime of belongings under pressure, in a weekend, while grieving. Share. Talk about heirlooms now, while everyone can hear the stories behind them. Here is something that surprises many parents: adult children usually want far less than you expect. That conversation is so much easier at the kitchen table today than in the middle of a move. And if it all feels like too much, a senior move manager can help you sort, sell and donate. Activate. One drawer, one closet, one box a week. Make four piles in every room: • Keep what you use and love every day. • Gift heirlooms now, so you can see them enjoyed. • Sell pieces of value that no one in the family will use. • Donate everything else, so it can start a new life somewhere. Your Next Best Chapter Check out the Piedmont Adult School catalog out on December 6, 2026, and join Debbi on January 30, 2027, at Piedmont Adult School for her one-day course. Planning ahead can make life’s next chapter easier, more organized, and less stressful. Debbi’s class is designed for seniors and their families to help you prepare for the future with confidence— long before a move becomes necessary. Debbi DiMaggio and trusted guest experts will share practical guidance on downsizing, preparing your home for the future, organizing wills and estate documents, and protecting yourself from scams targeting seniors. You’ll leave with a practical Get-It-In-Order Checklist and one simple, actionable next step you can take right away. articles.text: The Piedmont Seniors got into the spirit of the ’50s as they ventured to Jack London Square for an outing on the USS Potomac to take a Bay cruise that featured a special appearance by Elvis Presley (or at least an impersonator)! Before boarding the USS Potomac, the group visited the USS Potomac’s Visitor Center, where they watched a video highlighting the history of the ship. Built in 1934, it was originally the Coast Guard cutter Electra. It was renamed and converted to the Presidential Yacht USS Potomac by Franklin D. Roosevelt as a US Navy vessel in 1936. Cruising on the Potomac allowed the 32nd US president to get away from the formalities and stress of the White House. We don’t plan the next twenty years. I share that line every time I speak with seniors and their families, and the room always goes quiet. When I ask who has booked a restaurant for a trip months away, hands shoot up. When I ask who has a written plan for where they will live, who will manage things, and what will happen to everything in the house, very few hands go up. In more than 35 years as a realtor, I have walked alongside so many families through a parent’s move, a loss, or a long overdue downsizing. Right now we are working with four families in which the wife is living with dementia, and it has fallen to the husbands and the children to figure out what comes next. More often than not, that conversation turns into an argument. The difference between a stressful transition and a peaceful one almost always comes down to one thing: when they started. That is why I created Your Next Best Chapter, a one-day course for seniors and the families who love them, taking place January 30 at Piedmont Adult School. Nothing about planning ahead requires a decision today. It simply requires getting started. The way I help people get started is the same way I trained for my first marathon, a few months shy of my 60th birthday. I was not a runner at allbut I had the Mindset In Motion Method™. Earlier this year I published Mindset In Motion™: Activate Purpose, Power, and Peak Performance. Since then, I have been sharing the core concept of the book, the Mindset In Motion Method™, a five-step framework to help you through any transition: overcoming a loss, moving into a new chapter, conquering a personal or professional goal, or simply pushing yourself to Activate. So, take out a notepad and start outlining a plan for your future, while you are still in control of it. Five Steps, Any Goal • Goal. Get clear on exactly what you want. • Believe. Tell yourself it is possible, and that it is never too early to begin. • Internalize. Feel how it will feel once you are there. • Share. Bring in the people who will help you. • Activate. Take one concrete step this week. Here is how it works for two of the biggest pieces of any next chapter. Here’s one example: Purging • Goal. Picture a home filled only with the things you use and love every day. Not • • • • empty, just lighter. Believe. You do not need a moving date to begin. In fact, having no deadline is a gift. The people who feel the least stress on moving day are the ones who started years before, a little at a time. Internalize. Imagine opening a closet and seeing only what matters. Imagine the peace of knowing your children will never have to sort through a lifetime of belongings under pressure, in a weekend, while grieving. Share. Talk about heirlooms now, while everyone can hear the stories behind them. Here is something that surprises many parents: adult children usually want far less than you expect. That conversation is so much easier at the kitchen table today than in the middle of a move. And if it all feels like too much, a senior move manager can help you sort, sell and donate. Activate. One drawer, one closet, one box a week. Make four piles in every room: • Keep what you use and love every day. • Gift heirlooms now, so you can see them enjoyed. • Sell pieces of value that no one in the family will use. • Donate everything else, so it can start a new life somewhere. Your Next Best Chapter Check out the Piedmont Adult School catalog out on December 6, 2026, and join Debbi on January 30, 2027, at Piedmont Adult School for her one-day course. Planning ahead can make life’s next chapter easier, more organized, and less stressful. Debbi’s class is designed for seniors and their families to help you prepare for the future with confidence— long before a move becomes necessary. Debbi DiMaggio and trusted guest experts will share practical guidance on downsizing, preparing your home for the future, organizing wills and estate documents, and protecting yourself from scams targeting seniors. You’ll leave with a practical Get-It-In-Order Checklist and one simple, actionable next step you can take right away. She said many retired Piedmonters whose children have left home find they have few social outlets. One attendee, she said, was a woman who traveled from Oakland to sign up for activities and meet people. “I heard a lot of personal stories about how adult recreation and this event turned people on to something new,” Gardner said. Organizers plan to improve their outreach for future Expos and to collect stories from attendees about why they came. They hope to share those stories so seniors and empty nesters know others are in a similar position and that community activities are available to help them build a social network. Those interested in learning more about the organizations that attended the event can go to the city’s website: https://piedmont. ca.gov/news/events/adult_recreation_expo. City Administrator Rosana Bayon Moore and Communications Officer Echa Schneider hosted a table at the event to speak with residents about the work the city is doing.
